blocks.body:
Fermat knew that the odd primes of the form $x^2 + y^2$ are those $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and that the primes of the form $x^2 + 2y^2$ are $2$ and those $\equiv 1, 3 \pmod 8$. For $x^2 + 5y^2$ something new happens. The primes it represents are $5$ and those $\equiv 1, 9 \pmod{20}$, while the primes $\equiv 3, 7 \pmod{20}$, such as $3$ and $7$, are missed, even though for them $-5$ is still a square modulo $p$. They are caught instead by a second form, $2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$: indeed, writing $f(x,y) = 2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$, we have $3 = f(0, 1)$ and $7 = f(1, 1)$.

Lagrange and Gauss explained this by studying all forms $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ at once. Forms related by an invertible integer change of variables represent the same numbers, so the real objects are equivalence classes. For each discriminant there are finitely many classes, each with one reduced representative, and their number $h(D)$ counts the essentially different forms; $h(-20) = 2$.

blocks.title: Binary quadratic form
blocks.body:
A binary quadratic form is $f(x, y) = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ with integers $a, b, c$, written $(a, b, c)$. Its discriminant is $D = b^2 - 4ac$. The form is primitive if $\gcd(a, b, c) = 1$, and positive definite if $D < 0$ and $a > 0$; then $f(x, y) > 0$ for all $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$, since $4a f(x,y) = (2ax + by)^2 - D y^2$.

Note that $D \equiv b^2 \pmod 4$, so every discriminant is $\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.

blocks.title: Equivalence of forms
blocks.body:
If $\begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ \gamma & \delta \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, that is, the entries are integers and $\alpha\delta - \beta\gamma = 1$, then

$$g(x, y) = f(\alpha x + \beta y,\ \gamma x + \delta y)$$

is again a binary quadratic form, and $f$ can be recovered from $g$ by the inverse matrix, which also has integer entries. We call $f$ and $g$ properly equivalent. Equivalent forms represent exactly the same integers, because the substitution is a bijection of $\mathbb Z^2$.

They also have the same discriminant. Write $f(v) = v^{\mathsf T} M v$ with $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b/2 \\ b/2 & c\end{pmatrix}$, so $D = -4\det M$. The substitution $v = A w$ replaces $M$ by $A^{\mathsf T} M A$, whose determinant is $\det(A)^2 \det M = \det M$.

Two substitutions generate everything we need:

- $S: (x, y) \mapsto (-y, x)$ sends $(a, b, c)$ to $(c, -b, a)$.
- $T^k: (x, y) \mapsto (x + ky, y)$ sends $(a, b, c)$ to $(a,\ b + 2ak,\ ak^2 + bk + c)$.

For example $T^1$ turns $x^2 + y^2$ into $(x+y)^2 + y^2 = x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2$. The middle coefficient can be shifted by any multiple of $2a$; this is the key to reduction.

blocks.title: Which numbers does some form represent?
blocks.body:
Say $f$ properly represents $n$ if $n = f(x, y)$ with $\gcd(x, y) = 1$. A prime represented by a form is automatically properly represented, since $g = \gcd(x,y)$ gives $g^2 \mid f(x,y)$.

Lemma. The integer $n \ne 0$ is properly represented by some form of discriminant $D$ if and only if $D \equiv b^2 \pmod{4n}$ for some integer $b$.

Proof. If $f(p, q) = n$ with $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, choose integers $r, s$ with $ps - qr = 1$ (by [[bezout|Bézout's identity]]). The equivalent form $g(x, y) = f(px + ry,\ qx + sy)$ has $g(1, 0) = f(p, q) = n$, so $g = (n, b, c)$ for some $b, c$, and $D = b^2 - 4nc \equiv b^2 \pmod{4n}$. Conversely, if $D = b^2 - 4nc$ then $(n, b, c)$ is a form of discriminant $D$ with $f(1, 0) = n$.

Now take $n = p$ an odd prime not dividing $D$. Since $D \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$, the condition $D \equiv b^2 \pmod 4$ just says $b \equiv D \pmod 2$, and by the [[crt]] it can be combined with any condition modulo $p$. So: an odd prime $p \nmid D$ is represented by some primitive form of discriminant $D$ if and only if the Legendre symbol $\bigl(\frac{D}{p}\bigr) = 1$. (The form $(p, b, c)$ is primitive because a common factor would have to be $p$, and $p \mid b, c$ would give $p \mid D$.)

This is where [[quadratic-residues|quadratic reciprocity]] enters: it turns the condition $\bigl(\frac Dp\bigr) = 1$ into congruence conditions on $p$ modulo $|D|$. The remaining question, which form of discriminant $D$ represents $p$, is easy when there is only one class.

blocks.title: Reduced form
blocks.body:
A primitive positive definite form $(a, b, c)$ is reduced if

$$|b| \le a \le c,\qquad b \ge 0 \text{ if } |b| = a \text{ or } a = c.$$

The boundary conditions break the ties between $(a, b, c)$ and the equivalent forms $(a, -b, c)$ that occur when $|b| = a$ or $a = c$.

blocks.title: Reduction theorem
blocks.body: Every primitive positive definite form is properly equivalent to exactly one reduced form. A reduced form of discriminant $D$ satisfies $a \le \sqrt{|D|/3}$, so there are finitely many, and the class number $h(D)$, the number of proper equivalence classes of primitive positive definite forms of discriminant $D$, is finite.

blocks.title: Proof of the reduction theorem
blocks.body:
Existence. Start with any positive definite $(a, b, c)$ and repeat the following.

1. Apply $T^k$ with $k$ chosen so that $b + 2ak$ lies in the interval $(-a, a]$. This is possible because the interval has length $2a$. It does not change $a$.
2. If now $a > c$, apply $S$ to get $(c, -b, a)$, whose first coefficient is strictly smaller, and go back to step 1.

Each pass through step 2 strictly decreases the positive integer $a$, so the process stops, at a form with $-a < b \le a \le c$. If $a < c$, or $a = c$ and $b \ge 0$, it is reduced. In the remaining case $a = c$ and $b < 0$, apply $S$ once more: $(a, b, a) \mapsto (a, -b, a)$ is reduced. Primitivity is preserved by equivalence, since the coefficients of each form are integer combinations of those of the other.

Finiteness. If $(a,b,c)$ is reduced, then

$$|D| = 4ac - b^2 \ge 4a^2 - a^2 = 3a^2,$$

so $a \le \sqrt{|D|/3}$. Then $|b| \le a$ is bounded, and $c = (b^2 - D)/(4a)$ is determined by $a$ and $b$.

Uniqueness. First a lower bound for a reduced form $f = (a, b, c)$. If $|x| \ge |y|$, then $|bxy| \le |b|x^2$, so

$$f(x, y) \ge (a - |b|)x^2 + cy^2 \ge (a - |b| + c)\,y^2,$$

using $a - |b| \ge 0$. Symmetrically, $f(x, y) \ge (a - |b| + c)\,x^2$ when $|y| \ge |x|$. Since $a - |b| + c \ge c$, we get $f(x, y) \ge c$ whenever $xy \ne 0$, while $f(x, 0) = ax^2$ and $f(0, y) = cy^2$. Hence $a$ is the smallest nonzero value of $f$, and $f(x, y) = a$ with $y \ne 0$ is possible only if $a = c$.

Now let $f = (a, b, c)$ and $g = (a', b', c')$ be reduced, with $g(x, y) = f(\alpha x + \beta y, \gamma x + \delta y)$ for a matrix in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. They take the same values, so $a' = a$, and $f(\alpha, \gamma) = g(1, 0) = a$.

If $\gamma = 0$, then $\alpha\delta = 1$, so $\alpha = \delta = \pm 1$. Since $f(-x, -y) = f(x, y)$, the substitution acts as $T^k$ with $k = \alpha\beta$, so $b' = b + 2ak$. Both $b$ and $b'$ lie in $[-a, a]$, so either $b' = b$ or $\{b, b'\} = \{-a, a\}$, and the second option is excluded because a reduced form with $|b| = a$ has $b = a$. So $b' = b$, and $c' = c$ because the discriminants agree.

If $\gamma \ne 0$, then $f(\alpha, \gamma) = a$ forces $a = c$ by the first paragraph. The inverse matrix $\begin{pmatrix} \delta & -\beta \\ -\gamma & \alpha \end{pmatrix}$ sends $g$ back to $f$ and also has a nonzero lower-left entry, so the same reasoning applied to $g$ gives $a' = c'$. Then $b^2 = D + 4a^2 = b'^2$, and the boundary condition for $a = c$ makes $b, b' \ge 0$, so $b' = b$ and $c' = c$. In both cases $g = f$.

blocks.title: Reducing a form
blocks.solution:
The discriminant is $34^2 - 4 \cdot 10 \cdot 29 = 1156 - 1160 = -4$, and $a = 10 > 0$, so the form is positive definite.

Step 1: shift $b = 34$ into $(-10, 10]$ using $T^k$ with $k = -2$: the new middle coefficient is $34 - 40 = -6$ and the new last coefficient is $10 \cdot 4 + 34 \cdot (-2) + 29 = 1$. We now have $(10, -6, 1)$.

Step 2: $a = 10 > c = 1$, so apply $S$: $(1, 6, 10)$.

Step 1 again: shift $6$ into $(-1, 1]$ with $k = -3$: middle coefficient $6 - 6 = 0$, last coefficient $9 - 18 + 10 = 1$. We reach $(1, 0, 1)$, which is reduced.

So $10x^2 + 34xy + 29y^2$ is equivalent to $x^2 + y^2$, and represents exactly the sums of two squares. Since $(1, 0, 1)$ is the only reduced form of discriminant $-4$, we have $h(-4) = 1$, and every positive definite form of discriminant $-4$ behaves like this one.

blocks.title: Class numbers of -20 and -23
blocks.body: List the reduced forms of discriminants $-20$ and $-23$.
blocks.solution:
For $D = -20$ we need $a \le \sqrt{20/3} < 2.6$, so $a \in \{1, 2\}$, and $b$ even (since $b \equiv D \pmod 2$).

- $a = 1$: $|b| \le 1$ and even, so $b = 0$ and $c = 20/4 = 5$. Form $(1, 0, 5)$.
- $a = 2$: $b \in \{0, 2\}$ ($b = -2$ is excluded because $|b| = a$ requires $b \ge 0$). For $b = 0$, $c = 20/8$ is not an integer. For $b = 2$, $c = 24/8 = 3$. Form $(2, 2, 3)$.

So $h(-20) = 2$, with classes represented by $x^2 + 5y^2$ and $2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$.

For $D = -23$ we need $a \le \sqrt{23/3} < 2.8$, and $b$ odd.

- $a = 1$: $b = 1$ (as $b = -1$ has $|b| = a$), $c = 24/4 = 6$. Form $(1, 1, 6)$.
- $a = 2$: $b = \pm 1$, $c = 24/8 = 3$. Forms $(2, 1, 3)$ and $(2, -1, 3)$, both reduced because $|b| < a < c$.

So $h(-23) = 3$. The forms $(2, 1, 3)$ and $(2, -1, 3)$ are related by $(x, y) \mapsto (x, -y)$, which has determinant $-1$, but they are not properly equivalent. This is why proper equivalence is the right notion: with it, the classes form a group, and here it is cyclic of order $3$.

blocks.title: Primes of the form x^2 + 2y^2
blocks.body: Prove that a prime $p$ can be written as $x^2 + 2y^2$ if and only if $p = 2$ or $p \equiv 1, 3 \pmod 8$.
blocks.solution:
The form $x^2 + 2y^2$ has discriminant $-8$. For reduced forms of discriminant $-8$ we need $a \le \sqrt{8/3} < 2$, so $a = 1$, $b = 0$ (even, $|b| \le 1$), $c = 2$. Hence $h(-8) = 1$: every primitive positive definite form of discriminant $-8$ is equivalent to $x^2 + 2y^2$, and they all represent the same numbers.

$p = 2 = 0^2 + 2 \cdot 1^2$. For odd $p$, note $p \nmid 8$. By the lemma, $p$ is represented by some form of discriminant $-8$, hence by $x^2 + 2y^2$, if and only if $\bigl(\frac{-8}{p}\bigr) = 1$. Since $-8 = -2 \cdot 2^2$, this is $\bigl(\frac{-2}{p}\bigr) = \bigl(\frac{-1}{p}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{2}{p}\bigr) = 1$. By the supplementary laws, $\bigl(\frac{-1}{p}\bigr) = 1$ iff $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\bigl(\frac{2}{p}\bigr) = 1$ iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 8$. Checking the four odd classes modulo $8$:

$$p \equiv 1: (+)(+) = +, \quad p \equiv 3: (-)(-) = +, \quad p \equiv 5: (+)(-) = -, \quad p \equiv 7: (-)(+) = -.$$

So $p = x^2 + 2y^2$ exactly when $p \equiv 1, 3 \pmod 8$. For example $3 = 1 + 2$, $11 = 9 + 2$, $17 = 9 + 8$, $19 = 1 + 18$.

The same argument with $h(-4) = 1$ reproves Fermat's theorem on [[sums-of-squares]]. For $D = -20$ it only shows that primes $p \ne 2, 5$ with $\bigl(\frac{-20}{p}\bigr) = 1$, namely $p \equiv 1, 3, 7, 9 \pmod{20}$, are represented by one of the two reduced forms; separating $1, 9$ from $3, 7$ needs genus theory.

blocks.title: Composition and the class group
blocks.body:
For $D = -20$, the non-principal form $f = 2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$ satisfies $2f(x,y) = (2x + y)^2 + 5y^2$, and expanding shows

$$f(x, y)\, f(u, v) = X^2 + 5Y^2, \qquad X = 2xu + xv + yu - 2yv,\quad Y = xv + yu + yv.$$

So a product of two values of $f$ is a value of the principal form $x^2 + 5y^2$ (for instance $2 \cdot 3 = 6 = 1^2 + 5 \cdot 1^2$): the class of $f$ behaves like an element of order $2$.

Gauss (1801) defined such a composition for every discriminant. For $D < 0$ it makes the $h(D)$ proper classes of primitive positive definite forms into a finite abelian group, the form class group. Its identity is the class of the principal form $x^2 - \frac D4 y^2$ (if $D \equiv 0 \pmod 4$) or $x^2 + xy + \frac{1 - D}{4} y^2$ (if $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$). This was the first class group, decades before groups were defined.

The negative discriminants with $h(D) = 1$ are exactly the thirteen

$$D = -3, -4, -7, -8, -11, -12, -16, -19, -27, -28, -43, -67, -163.$$

Proving that the list is complete was a problem going back to Gauss. It was solved by Heegner (1952) and, independently, by Baker and Stark (1966–1967).

- Proper versus improper equivalence. Matrices of determinant $-1$ also preserve the set of represented numbers, but using them merges $(2, 1, 3)$ with $(2, -1, 3)$ and destroys the group structure. The class number $h(D)$ counts $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ classes.
- Forgetting the boundary conditions in the definition of reduced form, which leads to counting $(a, -a, c)$ and $(a, a, c)$ (or $(a, b, a)$ and $(a, -b, a)$) twice; these pairs are properly equivalent.
- Being represented by some form of discriminant $D$ is not the same as being represented by a given form, unless $h(D) = 1$. The congruence $\bigl(\frac{-5}{3}\bigr) = 1$ does not make $3$ a value of $x^2 + 5y^2$.
- Counting non-primitive forms: $(2, 0, 2)$ has discriminant $-16$ but is twice $(1, 0, 1)$; it is not counted in $h(-16)$.

Geometrically, a positive definite form measures squared lengths in a lattice: $f(x, y) = a\,|x + y\tau|^2$ with $\tau = \frac{b + \sqrt D}{2a}$ in the upper half plane. Changing the basis by $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ changes the form. The reduced form corresponds to a shortest basis, with $\tau$ in the standard fundamental domain $|\mathrm{Re}\,\tau| \le \tfrac12$, $|\tau| \ge 1$.

Algebraically, for fundamental $D < 0$ the form class group is isomorphic to the [[class-group|ideal class group]] of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt D)$, the form $(a, b, c)$ matching the ideal with basis $a, \frac{-b + \sqrt D}{2}$ (see [[ideals]]). Class number one for $D = -4$ and $D = -3$ is unique factorisation in the [[gaussian-integers]] and [[eisenstein-integers]]. Dirichlet's [[class-number-formula]] computes $h(D)$ from $L(1, \chi_D)$, where $\chi_D(n)$ is the Kronecker symbol $\bigl(\frac{D}{n}\bigr)$. For fundamental $D < -4$ it becomes $h(D) = -\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{a=1}^{|D|} \chi_D(a)\, a$. Indefinite forms ($D > 0$) have their own reduction theory, with cycles of reduced forms that are computed by the [[continued-fractions|continued fraction]] of a quadratic irrational, and their automorphisms come from [[pell|Pell's equation]].

1. Reduce the form $(7, 24, 21)$ and identify the reduced form you reach.
2. Find all reduced forms of discriminant $-56$ and show that $h(-56) = 4$.
3. Show that $h(-3) = 1$ and deduce that an odd prime $p \ne 3$ is of the form $x^2 + xy + y^2$ if and only if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.
4. Verify the composition formula for $2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$ above by expanding both sides.
